segments.title: Contemporary data needs a warship-modification caveat
segments.summary: A standardized 1934 reference puts carriers on common footing, but its as-built figures cannot capture every later alteration by governments, navies, crews, and sailors.
segments.body: The comparison uses a contemporary Institution of Naval Architects reference to put the carriers on a common statistical footing. Its published figures stay close to their as-built configurations, which makes cross-national comparison easier than mixing specifications from later refits. Warships rarely remain exactly as completed. Governments and navies authorize alterations, while crews and individual sailors make practical changes of their own. This caveat separates a controlled design comparison from the many configurations a ship may display during its service life.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the contemporary comparative source and warns that governments, navies, crews, and sailors modify warships after completion.

segments.title: Argus bridges experiment, training, and ferry work
segments.summary: HMS Argus links interwar experimentation with naval-aviation training and wartime aircraft-ferry missions to Malta, while her modest specifications set the decade's baseline.
segments.body: HMS Argus was completed in 1918 and became central to Royal Navy naval-aviation experiments during the interwar years. Her deployments to the Far East and other destinations extended that work beyond home waters. During World War II she served as a training carrier and ferried aircraft to Malta, where her large lifts proved useful. The contemporary figures give her a displacement of about 14,450 tons, a top speed of 20 knots, six 4-inch anti-aircraft guns, and roughly 15 aircraft. Those modest numbers provide a baseline for the larger carriers that followed during the decade.

evidence.note: Argus's experimental role, deployments, later training and Malta ferry work, dimensions, speed, armament, and air group are described.

segments.title: Early carriers solve launch and landing hazards
segments.summary: Rounded flight-deck bows, accelerators, restraining wires, barriers, and arresting gear show how launch and recovery systems changed as aircraft grew heavier.
segments.body: Argus's rounded bow improved airflow over a flight deck built before carrier catapults became standard. The Royal Navy called carrier-launch devices accelerators, while the term catapult still referred to equipment used on cruisers and battleships. Early longitudinal deck wires were intended less to stop a light aircraft than to keep it from blowing sideways after landing. Heavier aircraft made barriers and arresting cables necessary again for stopping an aircraft safely. That return followed the principle Eugene Ely had tested in an early landing experiment, although later systems replaced improvised sandbag weights with purpose-built gear. The sequence ties carrier handling equipment directly to changing aircraft weight and deck hazards.

evidence.note: The transcript explains rounded decks, accelerators, early deck wires, barriers, and arresting gear.

segments.title: Langley shows how funnels govern carrier islands
segments.summary: USS Langley's collier conversion shows how machinery position, exhaust trunking, flight-deck turbulence, and command redundancy shaped carrier islands.
segments.body: USS Langley was shorter, narrower, slower, and lighter than Argus, yet carried about 30 aircraft against Argus's 15. Her collier layout concentrated machinery aft and let simple external funnels preserve hangar volume, while Argus's converted-liner machinery required longer exhaust runs through the ship. Exhaust gases still had to clear flight operations without creating disruptive turbulence. An island could combine funnels with command positions and avoid extensive internal trunking. A 2021 South Korean carrier concept provides a modern comparison with Queen Elizabeth-class carriers and Italian LHDs: twin slim islands can serve separate exhaust paths. A second island also provides some command redundancy. This practical case for carrier islands does not make exposed command stations on the booms of fictional Venator-class spacecraft a sound warship arrangement.

evidence.note: Machinery, hangar space, exhaust routing, turbulence, and island arrangements are linked.

segments.title: Hosho and Eagle define different carrier scales
segments.summary: Hosho's compact purpose-built form contrasts with HMS Eagle's larger battleship conversion, heavy guns, smaller air group, and possible flagship role.
segments.body: Hosho was a compact but comparatively fast early carrier. At 7,470 tons, 25 knots, and 26 aircraft, she was smaller than Langley but 10 knots faster, while her island and funnel arrangement simplified flight operations. HMS Eagle displaced 22,600 tons, made 24 knots, mounted nine 6-inch and four 4-inch anti-aircraft guns, and carried 21 aircraft. Her air group placed her near the cruiser-carrier role, yet she served with fleets and on the Mediterranean and Far East stations. A photograph of Eagle accompanies an explicitly uncertain claim: the Prince of Wales's takeoff during a trip to Rio de Janeiro may have been the first such departure by an heir to a head of state. Her battleship origins suggested the potential for command space if a larger, later conversion had been possible, showing why islands grew in importance as carriers became capital ships and flag platforms.

evidence.note: Hosho and Eagle dimensions, air groups, roles, and island implications are discussed.

segments.title: Hermes gives the Royal Navy early carrier depth
segments.summary: HMS Hermes shows how a purpose-built carrier could support China Station deployment, a distributed British carrier force, and a balanced three-flight air group.
segments.body: Hermes was the first ship laid down as an aircraft carrier and already had a recognizably modern island-and-flight-deck arrangement. On her way to the China Station in 1924, she called at Honolulu, placing British carrier operations far beyond home waters. At about 10,850 tons and 25 knots, she carried six 5.5-inch guns, three 4-inch guns, and roughly 15 aircraft. At that point the Royal Navy could distribute about 51 aircraft among Argus, Eagle, and Hermes, while the US Navy's 30 carrier aircraft were concentrated in Langley. Hermes usually operated three flights built around fighters, reconnaissance aircraft, and either spotting or torpedo aircraft, an early attempt to balance carrier missions.

evidence.note: Hermes's construction, deployment, comparative fleet numbers, and air-group composition are described.

segments.title: Furious briefly becomes the leading carrier
segments.summary: HMS Furious's 1925 configuration combined 31-knot speed, a 35-aircraft group, and an almost flush deck, giving her a brief lead over rival carriers.
segments.body: After conversion, Furious was 786 feet long, displaced about 22,450 tons, and carried a much larger air group than Britain's first carriers. Her 90,000 shaft horsepower produced a top speed of 31 knots, while ten 5.5-inch guns, three 4-inch guns, and roughly 35 aircraft gave her substantial capability for 1925. The arrangement was effectively flush-decked except for a small control position forward and to starboard. Nothing rivaled her combination of size, speed, and air-group capacity until the Japanese and American battlecruiser conversions entered service about two years later. Her brief lead captures the pace of interwar carrier development.

evidence.note: Furious's 1925 dimensions, speed, armament, air group, and contemporary standing are reviewed.

segments.title: Lexington and Saratoga overtake Akagi in 1927
segments.summary: Akagi was formidable, but Lexington and Saratoga used battlecruiser hulls to deliver greater speed, size, and 80-aircraft groups at the end of the decade.
segments.body: Akagi entered service in 1927 at about 26,900 tons, with a top speed of 28.5 knots, ten 8-inch guns, twelve 4.7-inch guns, and 50 aircraft. The American conversions arrived with greater speed, beam, length, and aviation capacity. Lexington and Saratoga turned battlecruiser hulls intended to catch enemy ships into platforms whose aircraft could reach farther and faster. Their 180,000 shaft horsepower produced about 34 knots, and each ship carried roughly 80 aircraft. Those dimensions and air groups made them the decade's largest and most prestigious carrier units.

evidence.note: Akagi is compared with Lexington and Saratoga in dimensions, power, speed, guns, air-group size, and contemporary prestige.

segments.title: American carrier scale reshapes British planning
segments.summary: Britain still fielded more carriers, but Lexington and Saratoga helped frame the case for a large Royal Navy strike carrier in the Far East.
segments.body: Britain ended the 1920s with the numerical carrier advantage, but Lexington and Saratoga gave the United States the era's most prestigious individual units. In this interpretation, their capability helped push British planning beyond battle-carrier and cruiser-carrier concepts toward a true strike carrier. A comparable large carrier would matter if the Royal Navy had to contend in the Far East or measure itself against American carrier capability. Foreign warship performance could therefore change procurement requirements even while raw fleet counts still favored Britain.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts British carrier numbers with American unit prestige and links the comparison to British strike-carrier planning for Far Eastern operations.

segments.title: Courageous and Kaga show flight-deck layout choices
segments.summary: HMS Courageous's lower flying-off deck and Kaga's enormous funnel show how airflow, exhaust routing, and hangar access affected carrier capacity.
segments.body: Courageous used a lower flying-off position linked directly to the hangar, while the rounded upper deck improved airflow for launches. The arrangement moved fighters from enclosed storage to a launch position without occupying the main landing deck. At about 22,500 tons, she made 30.5 knots, mounted sixteen 4.7-inch guns, and carried roughly 50 aircraft. Kaga's converted battleship hull offered great width and a 60-aircraft group, but her enormous exhaust trunk and funnel consumed space and topweight. She made 23 knots and carried ten 8-inch guns and twelve 4.7-inch guns. Removing the trunking and fitting an island might have raised her capacity from 60 to about 70 aircraft. Exhaust design placed a direct constraint on striking capacity.

evidence.note: Courageous's deck arrangement and Kaga's dimensions, air group, and funnel penalty are explained.

segments.title: A decade turns experiments into capable carriers
segments.summary: In less than ten years, experimental conversions gave way to larger, faster carriers with more efficient flight operations and stronger air groups.
segments.body: Judging 1920s carriers by the absence of later jet-age features hides the pace of development. In less than a decade, navies moved from experimental conversions toward very large, fast ships with more efficient flight operations and powerful air groups. Propulsion, exhaust routing, hangars, flight decks, and mission requirements produced several competing designs because no single solution had yet prevailed. The result was a concentrated period of naval experimentation in its own right.

evidence.note: The transcript emphasizes rapid development in carrier operating efficiency and capability across less than a decade.

segments.title: Carrier doctrine shapes hangars and air-group size
segments.summary: British plans favored maintenance and endurance for a long commerce war, while American and Japanese plans emphasized a concentrated first strike and rapid aircraft replacement.
segments.body: Different operating assumptions produced the varied 1920s designs. British planners reserved more maintenance space to keep carriers available during a long commerce war and counter-raider operations. American and Japanese planning increasingly emphasized a large initial strike, which encouraged bigger air groups and partly disassembled replacement aircraft stored overhead. Crews could bring those spares down and assemble them after losses or when other aircraft became unserviceable. The United States appeared best positioned to sustain that replacement flow through industrial production. Carrier capacity therefore reflected assumptions about war duration, maintenance, losses, and national industry as much as deck and hangar design.

evidence.note: National design strands are tied to maintenance, commerce warfare, strike concentration, spares, and industrial capacity.
